vocabGaps.why: 'mantra-recitation' is an Indic term. The PGM's core act is the recitation of a logos built from voces magicae / onomata barbara — untranslatable strings, divine-name chains and vowel sequences. Typing it 'mantra-recitation' imports the wrong tradition; typing it 'invocation/evocation' loses the fact that the formula is a FIXED TEXT copied verbatim in the handbook. Proposed culture-neutral type.
The Mithras Liturgy specifies non-lexical vocalizations (hissing, popping) alongside vowel-strings. No controlled type covers non-lexical sound-production as a ritual act (S2).

PGM IV.475–829 is a graded seven-stage ascent through elemental, aerial, planetary and supra-celestial ranks. 'visualization' captures the imagery and 'invocation/evocation' the speech, but neither captures the GRADED SEQUENCE with named gates — the structural feature that makes it a liturgy rather than a spell (S2).
'coercive-rite' names the intent but not the medium: an inscribed lead tablet deposited in a grave or well is a distinct procedural form with its own archaeology (S25).

Modelling a figure in wax or clay as a ritual object is not consecration-of-object (it is not consecrated), not yantra-construction (it is three-dimensional and iconic), and not covered anywhere (S25).

'offering/homa' is a Vedic fire-oblation term. PGM recipes specify bird sacrifice and blood use; Iamblichus Bks IV–VII is an extended DEFENCE of animal sacrifice. Forcing this into offering/homa erases both the act and the ethical register (S4, S21).

vocabGaps.gap: lecanomancy / lychnomancy / scrying (bowl, lamp, vessel divination)
vocabGaps.why: Confirms the inventory agent's flagged gap. PDM xiv's divination spells and the PGM's direct-vision recipes work through a bowl, a lamp or a medium's eyes. Collapsing them into 'divination-procedure' loses the apparatus (S4, S10).
A large PGM/Coptic recipe family and a category in Iamblichus Bk III; no controlled type (S10, S21).

PGM VII carries a Homer Oracle: a numbered-lot lookup table against verses of a canonical poem. Structurally identical to later Sortes and to bibliomancy; not 'divination-procedure' generically (S11).
The recipes' multi-day food, drink and sexual abstinence conditions are a PRECONDITION with duration, not the 'purification' rite itself. Same loss the inventory agent flagged for ascetic regimen.

The choice of substance is itself governed and is the theoretical heart of both the Cyranides (letter → plant/bird/fish/stone tetrad) and Proclus' sunthēmata doctrine. No type covers 'selecting the correspondent substance' as a procedural step (S19, S23).
Typed here as yantra-construction faute de mieux; charaktēres are non-alphabetic ring-lettered signs with no Indic diagrammatic geometry. (Deliberately not reproduced in this file.)
'consecration-of-object/talisman' presumes a consecration act; many PGM/Coptic amulets are simply written and worn or folded and deposited (S5).

The Leiden/Stockholm papyri are procedure-dense but their operations are artisanal chemistry, not 'alchemical-operation' in the transmutational sense — the tradition's own boundary is exactly what is at stake in the scholarship (S16, S17).

The single biggest completeness lesson in this slice. Iamblichus' De mysteriis and Proclus' On the Hieratic Art discuss, classify and JUSTIFY ritual at length while giving no executable sequence. They need a node role ('meta-procedural') distinct from a graded procedure — otherwise the graph either falsely credits them with procedures or falsely records them as procedure-free.

works.structuralFinding: THE ANATOMY OF A RECIPE (the round's structural deliverable, stated descriptively). A PGM formulary entry is built from a small, repeating set of SLOTS: (1) a TITLE/claim of effect; (2) MATERIA — the substances and objects required, often including an ousia, a substance sympathetically linked to the target; (3) an APPARATUS/support — lamp, bowl, tablet, ring, papyrus strip, figurine; (4) the ACTION — what is done with them; (5) the TIMING — hour, lunar day, planetary day, sunrise/sunset; (6) a PLACE/purity CONDITION — often a multi-day abstinence regimen preceding the act; (7) the LOGOS — the fixed spoken/written formula, frequently marked off in the manuscript and in bilingual books written in a DIFFERENT SCRIPT AND LANGUAGE from the surrounding instructions; and (8) a DISMISSAL or closing note. Recipes vary in which slots they fill; the slot-count filled is the best objective completeness metric available for this corpus and is what the completeness grades below track. This file records the slot inventory and never the slot contents.
works.bilingualFinding: In the bilingual handbooks the division is functional and consistent: Greek carries the RITUAL INSTRUCTIONS, Egyptian (Demotic, hieratic or Old Coptic) carries the INVOCATIONS. Language choice is itself a structural marker of the praxis/logos boundary — the clearest formal evidence that ancient compilers themselves distinguished 'what you do' from 'what is said'.

Purity requirements are stated as conditions rather than set out as rites — the pattern documented explicitly for PGM IV (S4) and treated here as the corpus norm.

works.title: PGM IV — the Great Magical Papyrus of Paris / Great Paris Magical Codex (= GEMF 57)
works.shelfmark: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, suppl. gr. 574
works.atlasNote: Should hang under the planned `pgm-corpus` entry rather than claim its own slug, unless the atlas admits per-papyrus nodes.

works.physicalDescription: Papyrus codex; 36 leaves/sheets giving 72 pages, of which 66 are inscribed; written on both sides; 3,274 lines; page height 27–30.5 cm, width 9.5–13 cm. The longest magical handbook surviving from antiquity — equivalent in text-volume to four or five ordinary papyrus rolls.
works.contentsProfile: Over 50 individual sections, the majority of them ritual instructions. Subject range: divination, erotic attraction and binding, favour-gaining, business success, anger-restraint, exorcism. NOTABLY ABSENT: medical magic. Also carries non-recipe matter — a reusable prayer, astrological data, plant-gathering lore, a salutation.

procedures.evidence: PGM IV.5–51 (the bilingual 'direct-vision' recipe) fills every structural slot the corpus offers: a stated purpose (theophany/face-to-face encounter), a multi-day purity precondition, a compounded eye-preparation with a named applicator, a lunar-day + sunrise timing, a specified ground-condition, an animal sacrifice with a disposal instruction, an immersion with a departure condition, and a recited invocation naming the powers. This is the strongest 'complete' grade in the slice: no step is deferred to an initiator and none is marked as withheld. (Recorded as slot-inventory only; the contents of the slots are deliberately not given here.)

The logoi are written out verbatim in the manuscript — that is what a formulary IS. Bilingual recipes write the invocation in Old Coptic-Egyptian while the surrounding instructions stay in Greek, so the boundary of the spoken text is physically marked in the manuscript.
Purity is imposed as a stated precondition with a duration (a seven-day period in the direct-vision recipe) but the manner of purification is assumed known, not described.
Animal offering appears as a required act with a species and a disposal, but the sacrificial protocol proper is assumed.

harm.note: Recipes specify the killing of birds and the handling of blood. Stated as historical content; no modern practice implied.

procedures.evidence: Phylactery/amulet elements appear inside larger recipes (e.g. the protective components of the ascent text's materia section); not itemised as a standalone consecration sequence in the sections examined.
See the segment record gem:pgm-iv-296-466.

works.preservationNote: The codex is exceptionally well preserved by corpus standards — it is the intactness of PGM IV, not its typicality, that makes it the default source for every popular account of 'ancient magic'. A survivorship-bias caveat the atlas should state.

works.title: PGM IV.475–829 — the so-called 'Mithras Liturgy'

titleDispute.positionA: Albrecht Dieterich, Eine Mithrasliturgie (1903), named it from its invocation of Helios-Mithras as the source of immortal revelation and read it as a genuine Mithraic cult document.
titleDispute.positionB: Franz Cumont rejected the Mithraic attribution: the text lacks Mithraic eschatology and the characteristic seven-sphere passage of the soul.
titleDispute.positionC: H. D. Betz: a text formed at the intersection of Greek, Egyptian and Mithraic traditions, its central ascent reflecting early Hermeticism.
titleDispute.positionD: Marvin Meyer: genuine Mithraic connections survive.
titleDispute.resolution: NOT RESOLVED. The name is a modern scholarly label with four live positions and must always be quoted with the 'so-called'. The r29 plan already anticipated this as a body-note ('Betz vs Cumont'); this round adds Meyer and Betz's own syncretic position, i.e. FOUR positions, not two.

works.structuralAnatomy: The single most articulated operative structure in the slice. Two clearly distinguished blocks: (a) ll. 475–750, a first-person ASCENT LITURGY in seven graded stages — elemental powers, lower aerial powers, planetary gate-guardians, a solar figure, seven asp-faced female Tychai, seven bull-faced male Pole-Lords, and a supreme figure appearing amid celestial phenomena, each stage carrying its own address; and (b) ll. 751–834, a following PRAXIS/MATERIA section giving the preparations (an insect-derived ointment, protective amulet elements, and a herb whose identification — kentritis — is itself a long-running botanical puzzle). The recipe block coming AFTER the liturgy block, rather than before it, is a structural fact worth recording: the manuscript treats the spoken/experiential text as primary and the material preparation as apparatus.

procedures.evidence: Every stage's address is written out; the sequence runs from opening to supreme encounter without a gap or an 'as you have been taught'.
Each grade is specified by its visionary content (what appears, in what form, with what attributes) — the imagery is prescribed in the text, not left to the operator.

The text specifies breath manipulation as part of the working (drawing in breath in coordination with the addresses) but does not set out a graded respiratory training; the technique is invoked as a component, not taught. Contrast the Indic prāṇāyāma manuals the repo already carries.

harm.note: Breath manipulation aimed at an altered state. Named as a documented hazard KIND per this round's harm-taxonomy requirement; described, never prescribed.

procedures.evidence: The ll.751–834 block names amulet and ointment components and their preparation as apparatus for the liturgy, but the amulet's own consecration is not separately set out.

The text frames itself as transmitting a revelation and claims a limited, quasi-initiatory transmission; it does not contain an initiation ceremony. This is a 'referenced' grade with positive evidence — the claim is made, the rite is not given.

works.claimNote: The tradition CLAIMS a temporary deification (apathanatismos, 'immortalisation') as the outcome. Recorded as the text's claim; no efficacy asserted or implied.

works.title: PGM IV.296–466 — an erotic binding/attraction rite (philtrokatadesmos / agōgē)
works.harmClass: COERCIVE — highest sensitivity record in this slice.
works.harmNote: This is a rite whose stated object is to compel a specific named person, overwhelmingly a woman named by a male operator, to abandon her household and come to him; the scholarly term agōgē designates precisely a spell that burns or torments its target in order to drive her out. It is admitted here ONLY as academic religious history and ONLY at the level of structure and typology, following the repo's abhicāra-wing precedent (Bühnemann's ṣaṭkarman variables mapped exhaustively and never assembled). NOTHING of its materia, formula, sign-set or sequence is reproduced. It should carry a page-level care note if it ever surfaces, and it must never be presented as an artefact of 'romance'.
works.structuralAnatomy: Structurally it is a THREE-MEDIUM rite: two modelled figurines (one an armed male deity, one a bound female target), pins driven into the effigy at named body-locations, and an inscribed lead tablet, with a formula recited and copied simultaneously. It is described in the literature as among the most detailed surviving instructions behind the several hundred curse tablets recovered archaeologically — i.e. it is one of the very few cases where a HANDBOOK RECIPE and its ARCHAEOLOGICAL PRODUCTS can be matched: a bound, pin-pierced female figurine in the Louvre corresponds materially to this recipe type.

procedures.evidence: Widely described as one of the fullest surviving binding instructions; formula, materia, effigy-treatment and tablet-deposition are all present in the text. Graded complete on that basis — a case where completeness and harm coincide, which is exactly why the grade must be recorded and the content must not.
The logos is written out in the handbook and is recited and inscribed at once.

works.scholarship: Faraone, 'The Ethnic Origins of a Roman-Era Philtrokatadesmos (PGM IV 296–434)' — note the line-range disagreement in the literature (296–434 vs 296–466), itself a recordable editorial fact.

works.title: The Coptic magical corpus
works.scale: Approximately 500–600 texts survive. Meyer & Smith, Ancient Christian Magic (1994), the largest published collection, holds about 100 — roughly one fifth of the corpus. The Würzburg Coptic Magical Papyri project (JMU Würzburg, from Sept 2018) is producing the first full edition (Papyri Copticae Magicae, vol. 1: Formularies, De Gruyter 2023) and the Kyprianos database (seven linked tables).
works.structuralFinding: THE MOST IMPORTANT METHODOLOGICAL FINDING OF THIS SLICE FOR THE COMPLETENESS DIMENSION. Magical papyrology already operates a hard binary that the repo's completeness grade half-reinvents: FORMULARY vs APPLIED TEXT. A formulary is a handbook of one or more recipes — titles, instructions, incense specifications, timings — and it marks its target with a PLACEHOLDER ('NN son/daughter of NN'). An applied text is the object actually produced in a performance — an amulet, a curse tablet, an inscribed vessel — and it carries a REAL NAME ('Jacob son of Euphemia'), and is often folded for wearing or deposit. Kyprianos counts, as reported: 181 definite formularies, 187 definite applied texts, 132 unclear, plus 45 uncertain formularies and 99 uncertain applied texts. TWO CONSEQUENCES FOR THE GRAPH: (1) applied texts are NOT procedure-bearing works at all — they are procedure OUTPUTS, and grading them for completeness is a category error the graph must be built to avoid; (2) the placeholder is a formal, machine-detectable marker of a text's operative status, which is a far better completeness signal than prose inference. The same project also observes that practitioners adapted formularies to circumstance rather than executing them verbatim — i.e. even a 'complete' recipe was not treated as a closed algorithm by its own users.

procedures.evidence: The formulary half of the corpus (181 definite) is by definition procedure-bearing with written-out formulae; that is what makes it a formulary in the project's own taxonomy.

Amulet production is the corpus's largest single output category — and uniquely in this slice, the PRODUCTS survive in bulk (187 definite applied texts), so recipe and artefact can be checked against each other.
Curse tablets are among the named applied-text types; the corresponding formulary recipes exist but were not itemised this round.

works.title: Leiden Papyrus X (P.Leid. I 397)
works.dateClaim: Written in Greek about the end of the 3rd c. AD.
works.provenance: Thebes; found in the early 19th c. by Jean d'Anastasi — the same acquirer as the magical papyri, which is why the alchemical and magical papyri are usually discussed as one find.
works.contentsProfile: 111 recipes. Subject: extracting or COUNTERFEITING precious metals, imitating precious stones, and purple dye; plus textile and ink recipes. The last eleven recipes are simply extracts from the Materia Medica of Dioscorides — a mineralogical appendix rather than operations.

procedures.evidence: 111 discrete recipes, each self-contained with materials and operations — a craft recipe book of the same formal type as a magical formulary but with no logos slot at all. Graded complete BECAUSE the absent slot is absent by genre, not by omission: nothing is said to be withheld and no initiation is invoked. The contrast with the PGM (which fills the same slots PLUS a spoken formula) is the cleanest structural comparison available in this slice.

harm.note: Greco-Egyptian metallurgical and colouring recipes of this class work with mercury, arsenic sulphides and lead compounds — all documented toxic and, in the case of mercury vapour and arsenic, hazardous by inhalation as well as ingestion. Named as a hazard kind. No substance list, proportion, temperature or sequence is recorded here, and none should ever be surfaced operationally: the repo's RASA_TOXICITY precedent applies directly.

procedures.evidence: Metal 'purification' language occurs but as a technical operation-name, not a ritual purification. Recorded to prevent a false type-match in the merged graph — a real de-duplication hazard for a synthesizer keying on the word.

genreDispute.positionA: These are technical/artisanal handbooks — craft chemistry of the goldsmith's and dyer's workshop, with no transmutational theory; their inclusion in 'alchemy' is a modern editorial decision going back to Berthelot's 1888 title.
genreDispute.positionB: They belong with the Greco-Egyptian alchemical tradition proper (pseudo-Democritus, Zosimos), share its vocabulary and its Theban milieu, and the 'imitation vs transmutation' line is anachronistic.
genreDispute.resolution: NOT RESOLVED. Flagged because the repo would otherwise have to choose a lane (alchemy-west vs a craft lane) and the choice is itself the scholarly question.

works.structuralAnatomy: A preface narrating the book's transmission (revealed to Noah by the angel Raziel, thence to Solomon — a legendary chain, recorded as the text's own claim), followed by SEVEN chapters, one per firmament. Each firmament is populated with its own ranks of angels — over 700 angel and archangel names in total — and carries the 'counsels' that use them: roughly 30 magical recipes.

procedures.evidence: Its c. 30 recipes are adjurations that name the specific angels of a specific firmament and are written out with their conditions; the text's whole architecture (angel catalogue → counsel) is designed so that a recipe is executable from the page. Described by a reviewer as showing magic to require 'extensive spiritual preparations, the proper magic implements, complex ceremonies, and a knowledge of the secret names of power' — i.e. the text supplies all four registers.
Purity and preparatory requirements are stated as conditions attached to individual counsels rather than set out as an independent rite.
Recipes involve inscribed implements and materials; itemisation not performed this round.
Dream-related and inquiry procedures are among the applications named.
Applications named in the literature include love spells and compulsion of animals/spirits alongside healing; the coercive register is present.

works.parallelFinding: A DOCUMENTED, NOT GUESSED, PARALLEL TO THE PGM: the text carries Greek technical terms (termini technici) and closes with a GREEK PRAYER TO HELIOS inside a Hebrew angelological handbook. This is the single most-cited piece of evidence that Greco-Egyptian and Jewish ritual literature shared a workshop culture, and it is the strongest PARALLELS edge available in this slice.

works.title: Cyranides / Kyranides
works.dateClaim: First compiled in the 4th c. CE, from earlier material — notably the treatise of Harpocration.
works.structuralAnatomy: Book I is an ALPHABETIC CONCORDANCE, not a recipe book: 24 chapters, one per letter of the Greek alphabet, each assembling a tetrad — a plant, a bird, a fish (broadly construed, including turtles and seals) and a stone — whose Greek names share that initial letter. The organising principle is the LETTER, and the resulting tetrads supply the materia for amulets. Books II–IV catalogue the properties of animals, birds, fish and stones.

procedures.evidence: Book I is a materia-selection apparatus rather than a set of rites: it tells a reader WHICH four substances go together and what is claimed of them, and amulet-making follows, but the fabrication and any consecration are thin or assumed. Waegeman's monograph is titled Amulet and Alphabet precisely because the amulet is reconstructed FROM the alphabetic scheme. Graded partial: the selection step is complete, the making step is not.
Magico-medical preparations are named across the books; no worked operation is set out.

harm.note: A magico-MEDICAL compilation. Its remedies are pre-modern pharmacology of no demonstrated validity and include animal and mineral materials. Historical description only — the repo's existing 'historical medicine, obsolete, described never prescribed' posture (used for Ficino's De vita) applies verbatim.

works.structuralFinding: The Cyranides is the slice's purest example of a text that is PROCEDURE-ADJACENT WITHOUT BEING A PROCEDURE MANUAL: it supplies one slot of the recipe anatomy (materia, chosen by a formal rule) at exhaustive length and leaves the other seven slots to the operator. Any completeness scheme that grades only whole works would misfile it; graded per slot it is exactly legible.

works.title: The Chaldean Oracles
works.atlasStatus: PLANNED in r29 §2.3 (lane alchemy-west, c. 170 CE; Psellos/Plethon/Ficino chain in body; Westcott 1895 PD witness with redaction flagged; Majercik cite-only) + tool T24 'Chaldean Oracles fragment browser' scheduled for R33. VERIFIED ABSENT from shipped data.

works.transmissionFinding: THE SLICE'S DEFINING FRAGMENTARY CASE, AND A DOUBLE LOSS. (1) The Oracles themselves survive only as roughly 300 fragments QUOTED by later writers — Damascius, Proclus, Simplicius, and the 11th-c. Byzantine Psellos. There is no manuscript of the work. (2) The commentaries that would have explained them — by Porphyry, Iamblichus AND Proclus — are ALL LOST. So the operative tradition survives at two removes: quotations selected by commentators, minus the commentaries that selected them. Every reconstruction of 'Chaldean ritual' is therefore an argument, not a reading.

procedures.evidence: Ritual language survives in the fragments but no continuous rite does; the quoting authors excerpted for doctrinal purposes, so the operative connective tissue is precisely what was not preserved. Fragmentary by the round's definition: survives only in excerpted form.
Fire- and light-imagery of the ascent is present in the fragments; no sequence survives.
The theurgic rites the Oracles underwrite (the anagōgē, the immortalising of the soul, the celebrated fire-and-light rites) are NAMED in and around the fragments and expounded nowhere that survives.
The tradition's trance-mediumship is asserted as the Oracles' own mode of production but not described procedurally in what survives.

works.title: De mysteriis — properly, the Reply of Abamon to Porphyry's Letter to Anebo
works.repoJoin: gw:iamblichus / work id 'de-mysteriis' in assets/js/core/data/greatworks.js — THE ONE WORK IN THIS SLICE ALREADY SHIPPED. Do not mint a new node; extend this one.
works.titleFinding: TWO SEPARATE EDITORIAL IMPOSITIONS, both of which the atlas should state, and the repo currently states only one. (1) THE TITLE 'De mysteriis' was bestowed by MARSILIO FICINO and has, in the Budé editors' phrase, burdened the text for over five centuries; the work's own title is the Reply to Porphyry's Letter to Anebo. (2) THE TEN-BOOK DIVISION is EDITORIAL, not authorial — devised by Scutelli for the 1556 Rome edition and perpetuated until Saffrey–Segonds (Budé, 2013); Wilder's 1911 English uses its own numbering, so every section reference must name its edition. Finding (2) is already in-repo (greatworks.js flag); finding (1) is NEW this round and belongs beside it.
works.structuralAnatomy: A defence, organised by Porphyry's questions rather than by any ritual order: the classes of superior beings and their apparitions; divination (dreams, oracles, divine inspiration, as against technical inference); the rationale of SACRIFICE and of Egyptian material rites; Egyptian theology and first causes; the personal daimon; and union/happiness.

procedures.evidence: THE SLICE'S CENTRAL COMPLETENESS CONTRAST, and the reason the assignment named it. De mysteriis is the fullest late-antique account of WHY ritual is held to reach the gods and contains, so far as this round's sources show, NO executable rite: it names, classifies and justifies invocation, sacrifice, statue-animation, divination and possession without setting any of them out. It is a THEORY of a practice whose manuals (the PGM) survive separately and anonymously. Grade: referenced, with positive evidence — the procedures are discussed at book length and given nowhere.

Book III (in the editorial division) is a period-native TAXONOMY of divination — dreams, oracles, divine inspiration vs technical inference. A classification, not a method. The repo already maps this chapter onto its four oracle tools as history.
Books IV–VII (editorial division) defend animal sacrifice and material rites at length without prescribing a sacrificial protocol.
Theurgic union is the work's stated goal; no initiatory sequence is given.

works.title: Proclus, On the Hieratic Art according to the Greeks (De arte hieratica)
works.transmissionNote: Survives as a short piece transmitted in the GREEK ALCHEMICAL manuscript tradition — its standard Greek text is in J. Bidez, Catalogue des manuscrits alchimiques grecs VI (1928). Its survival route is itself a finding: the one surviving Proclan text specifically on hieratic technique came down not through the philosophical manuscripts but through the alchemists' books, which is a documented (and rarely noted) bridge between the theurgic and alchemical corpora.

procedures.evidence: The treatise expounds the doctrine that underwrites statue-animation and talismanic practice — sympatheia binding the chain of beings, and sunthēmata/symbola as the divine tokens deposited in stones, plants, animals and images — and treats statues, incenses, purifications, invocations and epiphanies together with the philosophical concepts. It gives the RATIONALE for choosing a material, not an operation. Referenced, with the same positive evidence as De mysteriis.
Purifications are named among the ritual acts discussed; not set out.
Invocations and epiphanies are named and theorised; no formula or sequence.

works.theoreticalFinding: Proclus supplies the missing THEORY of the PGM's materia slot. The magical papyri specify an ousia — the sympathetically-linked substance — without ever saying why it works; Proclus' sunthēmata doctrine is the philosophical account of exactly that move. Recording the two together is the single most illuminating juxtaposition in this slice, and it is a doctrinal correspondence, NOT a transmission claim: nothing shows the papyri's compilers read Proclus (they mostly predate him) or that Proclus read them.

notes.razorCompliance: This file names procedure TYPES, counts recipes, grades completeness and inventories structural slots. It contains: no voces magicae or divine-name strings, no formula text in any language, no charaktēres or drawable signs, no quantities, no proportions, no temperatures, no substance lists for the toxic material, no ordered executable sequences, and no second-person address. Where a source supplied operational detail (materia identities, effigy treatment, dye chemistry) it has been abstracted to slot-level description. The four harm-bearing categories present — coercive erotic and cursing rites, animal sacrifice, breath manipulation, and toxic craft chemistry — each carry a named hazard KIND at the procedure row, per this round's requirement and the repo's abhicāra precedent.
schemaProposals: SEGMENT_OF (work-segment → work). PGM IV.475–829 and IV.296–466 are the slice's most important operative units and are NOT works; without this edge they either vanish or falsely become works. Line-range segments are the native citation unit of this entire corpus.
FOUND_WITH (work → collection) plus a `collection` node type. Archival co-provenance is a first-class, contested, citable fact here and is not expressible with any of the six given edge types.

A node ROLE of 'meta-procedural' for works that discuss/classify/defend procedure without containing it (De mysteriis, Proclus' hieratic treatise, the Letter to Anebo). Without it these works are either wrongly credited with procedures or wrongly recorded as procedure-free.

An `outputArtefact` node kind, or an explicit exclusion rule, for APPLIED TEXTS (amulets, curse tablets). They are procedure outputs, not procedure-bearing works; the Coptic corpus alone has 187 definite ones and grading them for completeness is a category error.

A `completenessBasis` enum on every CONTAINS_PROCEDURE edge — one of {slot-inventory, comparative-recension, self-contained-table, editorial-statement, genre-norm}. Every grade in this file rests on one of those five and they are not equally strong; recording the basis is what stops the grade being an opinion.
